name: World Humanoid Robot Games 100m sprint
ability_definition: The ability to quickly move the arms and legs.

task_realism.reasoning: Sprinting is a real, physical gross-motor task that exercises rapid leg cycling, so it is not a synthetic proxy. However, workplace uses of this ability mostly involve quick arm movements, such as fast reaching, grabbing, striking, sorting on lines, or emergency responses, or short bursts of leg movement in cluttered spaces. A straight-line 100m race on a track matches only a small part of how rapid limb movement is used at work.

evaluation_conditions.reasoning: The run takes place on a flat, standardized, obstacle-free track with a fixed distance and no concurrent task demands. Real work involves uneven surfaces, carried loads, interruptions, and safety constraints. The 2025 rules also allowed teleoperation for some entries, and it is unconfirmed whether the winning run was autonomous. That makes it unclear whether the score reflects the robot's own capability or a human operator's control. Hardware differences across teams add uncontrolled variance.

construct_coverage.reasoning: The ability is defined as quickly moving both arms and legs. The sprint measures only leg and locomotion speed. Even for the legs, finish time is confounded by stride length, balance and fall avoidance, actuator power, and gait control, not just limb movement speed. Arm speed, reaction-initiated movement, and short-burst limb speed are not captured at all.

format_match.reasoning: The input is an embodied physical task and the output is an objective, continuous time in seconds. This is a clean and meaningful measure of speed, unlike a multiple-choice or toy format. However, a single race time on a fixed course is a competition artifact rather than a work output such as tasks completed per minute or cycle time on a real operation.

transferability_reasoning: The WHRG 100m sprint is a genuine physical, objectively timed test of rapid leg movement, which gives it some face validity for Speed of Limb Movement. However, it ignores arm speed entirely, confounds limb speed with balance, stride, and hardware, and runs under idealized track conditions with possible teleoperation. It is best treated as a partial, low-to-moderate transfer proxy for how quickly a robot can move its limbs in real work.

2025.model_or_system: Tiangong Ultra (Beijing Humanoid Robot Innovation Center)
2025.metric: seconds (100m finish time; lower is better)
2025.human_reference: General working-age adults (the typical person who needs to move limbs quickly in work settings, e.g. manual, service or safety roles). Neither trained sprinters nor elite athletes.
